anchors.fact: Punch was the first mixed drink based on spirits to become popular around the world. English traders in India were making it by the 1630s, sailors spread it, and from the 1670s to the 1840s a shared bowl was the drink of choice for much of the world. It's the ancestor of the Daiquiri and the Margarita.
anchors.meaning: Everyone's drink, before it was anyone's.

anchors.fact: The popular story says "punch" comes from the Hindi for "five" (five ingredients, Fryer, 1676). But around 1630 the English merchant Peter Mundy recorded its name as *chaar bakhra*, Hindi for "four shares". Origin not established.
anchors.meaning: The truer name counts the people, not the ingredients (interpretation).

anchors.fact: Oleo-saccharum: sugar left with lemon peels pulls out their oil and becomes a fragrant syrup (about 12 hours sealed). It was considered a pillar of proper punch from the late 1700s.
anchors.meaning: Care that takes time, done in advance for others.

anchors.fact: Punch was shared from bowls. Small "sneakers" were passed from person to person, at both humble and grand gatherings, with no restriction on who drank.
anchors.meaning: Nobody at the edge of the room.

anchors.fact: Some punch bowls carried inscriptions inside that appeared as the bowl was emptied, like "Drink Fair" and "One Bowl More & then".
anchors.meaning: Messages for the ones who stayed until the end.

cocktail.closingLine: Ladle it out, and keep one cup back for yourself.
cocktail.glassware: a punch bowl with one big block of ice, ladled into small cups
method: The night before: bury the lemon peels in the sugar in a sealed jar and leave them alone. By morning the sugar will have pulled the oil out of the peels and turned into a fragrant syrup.
Stir the lemon juice into the jar until the sugar dissolves, then remove the peels.
Pour the lemon syrup, the rum and the cold tea into a punch bowl over one big block of ice. Stir.
cocktail.name: Four Shares

recipe.item: lemons, peeled in long strips (no white pith)

cocktail.tagline: The world is kinder with you in it.

reading.epigraph: This drink was never poured for one.
whoYouAre: You believe the best of people, and you'd rather be disappointed now and then than live any other way. You forgive quickly. It isn't that you don't notice. It's that holding on to it costs more than it's worth. When things go wrong for someone, you don't make a speech. You just stay. People feel safer around you, and they often couldn't tell you why, they just do.
Here's the part you struggle to show: you worry about being the one left out, the one who said the wrong thing, the one who let somebody down. So you make sure nobody else ever has to feel that way.
yours: Nobody knows exactly where punch was born. What we do know is that in the 1600s, English traders in India were mixing the local spirit with water, sugar, citrus and spice, and that sailors carried the habit to every port they reached. For almost two hundred years, a shared bowl of punch was the drink of choice across much of the world. It was the first mixed drink with spirits to travel the globe, and it's the ancestor of drinks you know, like the Daiquiri and the Margarita.

Even its name is a small mystery. The story most people tell is that "punch" comes from the Hindi word for five, for its five ingredients. Maybe. But one of the first Englishmen to write the drink down, a merchant in India around 1630, recorded it under a Hindi name that means "four shares". I like to think that's the truer name: not what goes into it, but how many people get some.

Punch was never a drink for one. It was made in a bowl and passed around. Small bowls went from hand to hand, in taverns and grand houses alike, and anyone in the room could drink. Some bowls even had words painted inside that only appeared once everyone had had their share: "Drink fair." "One bowl more." That's you, isn't it? You're the one who makes sure the bowl comes round to everybody, and that nobody is left standing at the edge of the room.

So I made your punch the old way, the way that takes time, to honour the time you give to others. It starts the night before: strips of lemon peel buried in sugar and left alone until the sugar has drawn out all their oil and turned into a fragrant syrup. You can't rush it. You can only give it time. Then lemon juice, a bottle of aged rum and cold black tea, poured over one big block of ice and ladled into cups. It isn't clever. It's generous. It's a drink that says "I was thinking of you yesterday."

Here's what I'd ask of you. Make this one day for people you love, and don't wait for a reason. And the next time you're the one who's struggling, let someone pass the bowl to you. You've spent a long time making sure nobody is left out. You're allowed to be looked after too.
